Q100. End-to-end architecture challenge 
Processing sequence. The upgrade is a SOM change order with a mid-cycle effective 
date. ODI distributes it: the FI-CA provider contract gets a new item version, and CC 
ends the old charge plan and activates the new one, prorating recurring fees. Millions of 
usage events pass through Convergent Mediation, which de-duplicates and enriches 
them, and CC rates them against the valid tariff, consuming the prepaid balance online. 
When the balance is exhausted, policy either blocks usage or triggers a SOM change to 
postpaid. After the switch, CC rates usage offline and produces charged items as BITs 
for CI. 
The retroactive discount triggers rerating in CC or a CI discount, generating credit BITs. 
CI bills and invoices them, posting the receivable to FI-CA. The customer disputes the 
invoice, creating a dispute case with a dunning lock.

Q02. Subscription product modelling 
Model one sellable subscription product with three charge elements, and keep 
ownership clean. SOM owns the commercial offer: product master, contract term, add-
on options, price agreements visible to sales and the contract parameters (for example, 
committed quantity). CC owns the rating logic: a charge plan containing a recurring 
charge (₹40,000 monthly), a one-time activation charge (₹75,000 on contract start) and 
a usage charge with its rate tables. Add-ons are optional sub-products or additional 
charge plans activated through the order, each with its own effective date. CI owns 
billing behaviour: billable item class, item types for recurring, one-time and usage, 
billing cycle and invoice grouping.

charge-plan parameters, so define them once, with matching technical names and

answer_response.summary: The billing failures stem from three distinct architectural breaks: (1) Duplicate activation fees are caused by non-idempotent interface handling during a restart or re-trigger, where the one-time charge event was resent and accepted twice by CI; (2) Usage miscalculation likely results from incorrect tier mapping or missing mediation de-duplication, leading to rated quantities that do not match the 150 GB allowance threshold; (3) FI-CA posting failures indicate a break in the billing-to-accounting interface, often due to missing master data (contract account) or validation errors in the billable items (BITs) preventing the creation of receivables. Remediation requires targeted reprocessing of only error/unbilled items, leveraging BIT status to prevent duplication, and correcting the interface idempotency controls.

sections.title: Root Cause Analysis: Duplicate Activation Fees
Root Cause Analysis: FI-CA Posting Failures

claims.text: Duplicate billing of one-time activation fees often occurs when an interface restart causes the sender to resend an event without receiving an acknowledgement, and the receiver (CI) accepts both instances because it lacks idempotency controls.

The activation charge is a one-time charge triggered by the contract activation event in CC, which flows to CI as a billable item; if the event is resent, CI may create duplicate billable items unless source references are checked for uniqueness.

Usage charges are rated per chargeable item from mediation; miscalculation can occur if the mediation layer fails to de-duplicate events or if CC rates against the wrong tariff tier, resulting in incorrect quantities or prices.

FI-CA posting failures can be caused by billable items (BITs) stuck in 'raw' status due to validation errors such as missing contract account, invalid item type, or wrong currency, preventing the creation of receivables.

Section 1: End-to-End Data Flow Architecture across all 4 BRIM Pillars
A comprehensive operational walkthrough of the complete SAP BRIM transaction lifecycle:
1. Quote & Order (SOM): Customer accepts Solution Quotation (PRQ); Provider Order (PRVO) is
confirmed and released.
2. Order Distribution (ODI): Provisioning activates Provider Contract in SOM (PRVC), subscriber
contract in CC, and contract account links in CI/FI-CA.
3. Real-Time Consumption & Rating (CC): Network sends usage event via Diameter/Web Service.
CC Guider locates contract via UTI; CC Rater executes price plan; CC Updater updates
wallet/counters; CC Bulkloader outputs Billable Items.
4. Billing (CI): Mass run FKKBIX_BILL_M groups billable items into Billing Documents.
5. Invoicing (CI): Mass run FKKBIX_INV_M merges billing documents, applies clearing control,
creates Invoicing Document (ERDK) and posts open items to FI-CA (DFKKOP).
6. Receivables & Payments (FI-CA): Payment lot (FP05) or Direct Debit (FP35) clears open items via
Clearing Control (Posting Area 0150).
7. General Ledger Transfer: Mass run FPG1 transfers closed reconciliation keys to General Ledger
(ACDOCA/BSEG).
8. Statutory Revenue Recognition: CI transfers RAIs to SAP RAR (FARR_RAI_MON) for IFRS 15
compliance.
Reference: SAP BRIM Technical Standard - BRIM End-to-End - Section 1

SOM-16 — Functional design document outline 
An implementation-ready FDD for activation, recurring billing, mid-cycle upgrade, 
renewal and termination contains these sections. (1) Scope and business requirements 
with IDs. (2) Process flows for each lifecycle event, from order to invoice. (3) Business 
rules: activation date rule, proration rule (daily, by calendar days), upgrade effective

account and billing cycle to CI, external references from CRM.

and error handling. (6) Exception handling: distribution failure, rating failure, billing 
block, retry and owner of each queue. (7) Authorisations and segregation of duties. (8) 
Reporting and reconciliation: contract counts, billed amount versus expected.

architecture is SOM plus CI and FI-CA, with recurring charges generated without SAP 
CC, or a light CC charge plan setup, and usage either uploaded as billable items directly 
into CI (from a simple preprocessing step) or charged in CC without CM. 
What can be omitted: CM, if usage volume is low and sources deliver clean data (a 
simple upload or Integration Suite flow can validate and load); possibly CC, if pricing is 
fixed recurring and simple usage can be priced before upload. Cannot be omitted: FI-CA 
and CI (billing and receivables), and SOM if contract lifecycle changes are frequent. 
Required integrations shrink: no CM-to-CC flow; without CC, the price logic moves to 
the upload or to CI pricing, which is less flexible. 
Operational consequences: fewer components to run and patch, simpler 
reconciliation, lower licence and infrastructure cost. Limits: complex usage pricing, 
real-time balances or high event volumes become hard later. 
Scalability: keep the canonical billable item design compatible with CC output, so CC 
and CM can be added later without redesigning CI. Validate licensing implications with 
SAP.

Q100. End-to-end architecture challenge 
Processing sequence. The upgrade is a SOM change order with a mid-cycle effective 
date. ODI distributes it: the FI-CA provider contract gets a new item version, and CC 
ends the old charge plan and activates the new one, prorating recurring fees. Millions of

for CI.

answer_response.summary: The premise that CC posts usage directly to FI-CA, thereby eliminating the need for CI, is architecturally incorrect for standard SAP BRIM postpaid billing. In the canonical architecture, CC rates usage to produce charged items, which are transferred to CI as billable items. CI then performs billing and invoicing, and it is CI that posts the resulting receivables to FI-CA. While simplified architectures may bypass CC for simple recurring charges, CI remains a mandatory component for billing and receivables management, and bypassing CI to post directly from external events is explicitly identified as skipping necessary controls.

sections.title: Architectural Correction: The Role of CI in the Billing Flow
Standard Data Flow: CC to CI to FI-CA

claims.text: Creating FI-CA receivables directly from external usage events skips the controls that CI exists to provide, indicating that direct posting from usage sources to FI-CA is not the standard or recommended architectural path.
In the standard postpaid flow, CC rates usage and sends billable items to CI, while FI-CA holds the receivables; CI is the intermediary that processes these items into invoices.
The end-to-end processing sequence involves CC producing charged items as billable items for CI, which then bills and invoices them, posting the receivable to FI-CA.

CI posts through FI-CA, where business partner and contract account hold the customer's receivables; invoicing creates an FI-CA posting document with the receivable on the contract account and revenue and tax lines.
Even in simplified architectures where CC is omitted for fixed recurring pricing, CI and FI-CA cannot be omitted, as they are required for billing and receivables.

organization considers to be entitled to pass the good or service promised. The calcula-
tion of the allocated transaction price is handled by SAP Revenue Accounting and 
Reporting and is calculated as follows: 
(Total SSP of the POB +Total SSP of the SAP Revenue Accounting and Reporting contract) 
x (Total transaction price of the contract) = Allocated transaction price of the POB 
For Martex, the allocated amounts are $1,096.37 and $2,120.30 for the two POBs, as 
noted in Table 7.8. 
SAP Revenue Accounting and Reporting automatically calculates the allocation of 
POBs at SAP Revenue Accounting and Reporting contract creation.

Pricing 
In a typical SAP Billing and Revenue Innovation Management implementation, as 
mentioned previously, there are different types of pricing: 
• Pricing for a one-time charge 
• Pricing for a recurring charge 
• Pricing for a usage-based charge 
Customers will be charged a one-time, recurring, or usage-based subscription charge 
based on the service they subscribe to and consume. This offers more flexibility in set-
tlement of charges. For example, a mobile service provider offers services for custom-
ers such as a data plan based on usage consumption and voice and text messaging with 
a fixed monthly recurring charge; in addition, a one-time charge is usually applied for 
a new customer to activate services.

Subscription orders support different kind of products:
Subscription products
Subscription products can be used to subscribe to a service. Fees and charges can be 
managed in different ways. 
●
There are usage-based subscriptions for consumption, based pricing models for which the 
pricing is defined in SAP Convergent Charging.
●
There can also be products, which shall be billed on a regular basis, for example, monthly, 
the recurring subscriptions
●
There can also be one time fees, the one-off charges like an activation fee for a contract
All these subscription products are billed in SAP Convergent Invoicing as billable items. Billing 
documents are either being created directly in SAP Convergent Invoicing (recurring fees), 
being sent from Subscription Order Management (SOM) (one-off charges), or being sent 
from SAP Convergent Charging (usage based).
Physical goods
Physical goods can be treated as sales items, resulting in an SD sales order to support 
logistical processes, such as delivery or goods issue.
Bundles
Bundles can combine different kinds of products, to be sold in a bunch and to offer a specific 
process for the single bundle components. Bundles can be sales packages but also 
subscription products.

claims.text: SAP RAR allocates the transaction price to performance obligations based on the standalone selling price (SSP) of the POBs in the contract.
The formula for allocated transaction price is: (Total SSP of the POB / Total SSP of the contract) x Total transaction price of the contract.
SAP RAR automatically calculates the allocation of POBs at contract creation.
SAP RAR receives order (contract) and fulfillment and invoice data, allocates transaction price across performance obligations by standalone selling price, and posts revenue.
